passages.title: The sūrah's authority and the punishment for zinā
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Sūrah an-Nūr opens by announcing itself: Allah sent this sūrah down, made its rulings binding, and placed clear signs in it. Then comes the first command — the prescribed punishment for zinā (unlawful sexual intercourse) — and in ayah 3 a statement about who ends up marrying whom. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls the first verse an introductory preface placed there to put extra emphasis on the commands that follow.

## A sūrah that announces its own authority

**"A sūrah which We have sent down."** Ibn Kathir notes that Allah is pointing out the high esteem in which He holds this sūrah — which is not to say that other sūrahs are unimportant.

**"and which We have enjoined" (wa faraḍnāhā).** Mujahid and Qatadah explained this as: *We have explained what is lawful and unlawful, commands and prohibitions, and the prescribed punishments.* Al-Bukhari said that those who read the word as *faraḍnāhā* take it to mean, "We have enjoined them upon you and those who come after you."

**"and in it We have revealed manifest āyāt."** Ibn Kathir glosses *bayyināt* as *clearly explained*. Then the purpose: **"that you may remember."**

## Why this crime carries the heaviest penalty

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why zinā carries the heaviest of the punishments the Qurʼān prescribes: it is a great crime in itself and also a combination of many crimes, whose result is the destruction of the entire social order.

To violate a man's wife, daughter or sister is nothing less than his destruction. For a noble man, losing all his material wealth is not as bad as losing the chastity of his womenfolk. Where illicit sexual acts become rampant, family lineage is lost; and once the sanctity of relationship with mother, daughter and sister has vanished, marriage to them becomes conceivable — a crime greater still. Surveying the causes of disorder the world over, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges the root cause in most cases to be woman, and to a lesser degree wealth: only rules that safeguard both in a befitting manner, and do not let them cross the appointed limits, can guarantee worldly peace.

**The four ḥudūd.** The Qurʼān and *mutawātir* aḥādīth (reports transmitted by so many narrators that error is not credible) have between them fixed the punishments of four crimes, not left to the discretion of the judge or the ruler: stealing, levelling false accusation against chaste women, drinking liquor, and adultery. These fixed penalties are the *ḥudūd*. For every other crime the punishment is not fixed; the ruler or judge awards it according to the type of crime, the circumstances of the criminal, and the background in which it was committed — what Islamic jurisprudence calls *taʿzīr*.

## The command itself

**"Flog each one of them with a hundred stripes."** The verb *jalada* means to hit with the whip, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to its root: *jild*, leather. The Prophet ﷺ himself urged that whipping be exercised with moderation — neither so hard that it tears the flesh, nor so mild that it does not hurt at all. Ibn Kathir runs the same way: strike hard without causing a wound, so that the offender and others like him are deterred by the terror of it.

**Why the woman is named first.** The common practice in the Qurʼān's injunctions is that the command is conveyed by addressing the men, and women are included by implication. But here there was a real possibility that someone might suppose these injunctions relate to men only; so, as in certain other verses where women are named separately — *"and establish prayer and give zakāh"* (33:33) — an incidental mention was not considered enough. Then, having named her, the ayah puts her *first*, reversing the order kept in the theft ruling, where the male thief comes first (5:38). Women are the weaker sex, and compassion-able for their physique; had they not been mentioned specifically, one might have had the misgiving that they are exempt. And her nature has been bestowed with instinctive shyness and an urge to guard her chastity, so that reaching this act from her side requires extreme fearlessness — which makes it graver in her case. Theft is the mirror image: a man was given strength by Allah so that he might earn his living from the bounty Allah has provided, so stealing instead is the greater shame and sin for him.

## Pity, and what it may not do

**"Let not pity withhold you in their case, in a punishment prescribed by Allah."** Ibn Kathir: do not feel too sorry for them where the laws of Allah are established. What is prohibited is the kind of pity that may make the judge ignore the punishment altogether. Mujahid said: if the matter is taken to the ruling authority, the punishment has to be carried out and cannot be stopped — narrated likewise from Saʿid bin Jubayr and ʿAtaʾ bin Abi Rabah.

That the tenderness itself is no sin is underlined by a report Ibn Kathir gives from al-Musnad: one of the Companions said, "O Messenger of Allah, when I slaughter a sheep I feel pity for it," and the Prophet ﷺ answered that he would have a reward for that. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: pity, mercy, forgiveness and pardon are always laudable, but compassion shown to these criminals results in injustice to the whole of humanity.

**"if you believe in Allah and the Last Day."** Ibn Kathir reads this as the pivot: *then do that* — carry out the punishment.

## Made public

**"And let a party of the believers witness their punishment."** Ibn Kathir: this is more humiliating for the guilty if they are flogged in front of people, because it is more effective as a deterrent and conveys the sense of scandal and rebuke. Al-Hasan al-Basri glossed the phrase in a single word: *publicly*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that it is customary in Islam to carry out punishments — especially the ḥudūd — in public, so that onlookers take warning; but the directive that a group of Muslims be present is peculiar to this penalty.

Islamic law works hard to *prevent* vulgarity from spreading: women are obliged to cover, men to lower their eyes, and someone found falling short is to be guided in private, not disgraced. But once a person has crossed every limit and his crime is established, keeping it secret might embolden others.

## How the ruling arrived: three stages

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the injunctions on this crime were revealed gradually, moving from a lighter punishment to a more severe one, as with the gradual prohibition of alcohol.

**Stage one — Sūrah an-Nisāʾ 4:15–16.** Four witnesses were required; a woman proved guilty was to be confined to her home "until death overcomes them **or Allah prescribes a way for them**," and both parties were to be caused harm. This first penalty was *taʿzīr*, left to the discretion of the ruler or judge — which is why the deliberately open phrase was used, hinting that a further directive was coming.

**Stage two — this ayah.** ʿAbdullah Ibn ʿAbbas said that what was promised in 4:15 had now been prescribed: a hundred stripes for the man and the woman.

**Stage three — the Prophet's ﷺ elaboration.** Ibn ʿAbbas himself then made the hundred stripes exclusive to the unmarried: *stoning for the thayyib, flogging for the bikr* (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this from Sahih Bukhari, Kitāb ut-Tafsīr). Since this sūrah's wording gives the hundred stripes without qualification, he must have found it in another authentic ḥadīth — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names it: from ʿUbādah Ibn Samit, related by Sahih Muslim, Musnad Ahmad, Sunan Nasaʾi, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, in which the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Have knowledge from me, have knowledge from me: Allah has now prescribed the way"* — a hundred stripes and a year's exile for the unmarried, and for the married a hundred stripes and stoning.

On the year's exile the jurists differed — whether it is compulsory or at the judge's discretion; in the opinion of Imam Abu Hanifah it remains at the discretion of the ruler or judge. And although that ḥadīth mentions flogging before stoning for the married, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds — from other aḥādīth and the practice of the Prophet ﷺ and the first four Caliphs — that the two are not combined: the married offender is awarded stoning only. ("Married" is used here for ease; the technical terms are *thayyib* and *muḥṣan* — one who has had intercourse with a spouse in a valid nikāḥ, and who is free, adult and of sound mind.)

## From the Sunnah: the two bedouins

Ibn Kathir records — from the Two Sahihs, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah and Zayd bin Khalid al-Juhani — that two bedouins came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. One said that his son, employed by the other man, had committed zinā with his wife; the father had paid a ransom on his son's behalf of a hundred sheep and a slave-girl, but when he asked the people of knowledge they said his son should be given a hundred stripes and banished for a year, and that this man's wife should be stoned. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> *"By the One in Whose Hand is my soul, I will judge between you both according to the Book of Allah. Take back the slave-girl and sheep, and your son is to be given one hundred stripes and banished for one year. O Unays" — he said to a man from the tribe of Aslam — "go to this man's wife, and if she confesses, then stone her to death."*

Unays went to her; she confessed; the sentence was carried out.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the lesson: the Prophet ﷺ awarded a hundred stripes to one and stoning to the other, and described *both* as judgement by the Book of Allah — though Sūrah an-Nūr mentions only the stripes. The reason is that Allah had revealed to him the complete explanation and detail of the injunction, all of it falling within the purview of the Book of Allah even where this sūrah does not express it — *"it is nothing but revelation revealed"* (53:4).

## ʿUmar's sermon and the "verse of stoning"

Imam Malik recorded — and it is also in the Two Sahihs — that ʿUmar stood up, praised and glorified Allah, and said that among what was revealed to Muhammad ﷺ was the āyah of stoning, "which we have recited and understood." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ carried out stoning, and they did so after him; but ʿUmar feared that as time passed some would say they did not find stoning in the Book of Allah, and would go astray by abandoning an obligation Allah had revealed. He specified its conditions: a married man or woman, where decisive evidence is produced, or pregnancy results, or there is a confession. In the wording narrated by Nasaʾi he added that there is no avoiding this punishment, since it is one of the ḥudūd of Allah, and that were it not for the risk of people saying "ʿUmar has added to the Book of Allah what is not in it," he would have written it *in a corner of the muṣḥaf*.

If this were a verse of the Qurʼān whose recitation is mandatory like other verses, why would ʿUmar — well known for his vehemence about Allah's injunctions — leave it out merely for fear of people's calumny? And why speak of writing it on the *margin* rather than restoring it to its place? All this supports the inference that what ʿUmar had heard from the Prophet ﷺ was the authoritative explanation of this ayah, which he treated as belonging to the Book of Allah because of the Prophet's ﷺ words and consistent practice, while understanding that it was not itself a verse. The Prophet ﷺ carried it out on Māʿiz and on the Ghāmidiyyah in the presence of many Companions, and ʿAli likewise said that the verdict of stoning is established by the Prophet's ﷺ practice.

## Severe penalty, severe proof

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān insists that where Islamic law makes a punishment severe, it makes the conditions of proving the crime equally tough. Ordinary claims are established by the testimony of two men, or one man and two women. For the ḥadd of zinā, **four male eyewitnesses** are necessary, and they must testify without the slightest doubt or confusion; if the slightest uncertainty remains, the ḥadd is remitted and only a *taʿzīr* punishment commensurate with the crime may be awarded. And the witness carries his own risk: if his testimony is rejected, he may himself be charged with *qadhf* — false accusation — and awarded eighty stripes.

## Who ends up with whom

**Ibn Kathir's reading.** The *zānī* does not have intercourse except with a *zāniyah* or a *mushrikah* (a female idolator): no one would go along with him in this action except a sinful woman also guilty of zinā, or a woman who does not think it unlawful at all. By the same token, none marries the *zāniyah* except a *zānī*, or a *mushrik* who does not think it unlawful. Of *"Such a thing is forbidden to the believers"* Ibn Kathir says this means indulging in this, or marrying prostitutes, or marrying chaste women to immoral men; Qatadah and Muqatil bin Hayyan said that Allah forbade the believers from marrying prostitutes. He connects the ayah to the Qurʼān's conditions elsewhere that spouses be *"chaste, not committing illegal sex, nor taking boyfriends"* (4:25) and *"desiring chastity, not committing illegal sexual intercourse, nor taking them as girlfriends"* (5:5).

**From the Sunnah.** Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr that a man among the believers asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for permission to marry a woman known as Umm Mahzul, who used to commit adultery and who had made it a condition that she would spend on him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ answered him by reciting this very ayah. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Abu Hurayrah — and a similar report was recorded by Abu Dawud in his Sunan — that a *zānī* who has been flogged should not marry anyone except someone like himself.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges the simplest and safest meaning to be that the verse is not issuing a fresh injunction but describing a fact of life normally seen every day. Zinā is a poison to ethics; its poisonous effects ruin a man's moral behaviour until he stops distinguishing good from bad and no longer bothers about ḥalāl and ḥarām. Any woman he fancies, he fancies for this purpose; only if his advances fail does he agree to marriage, and then under compulsion, since he finds the real objects of marriage — faithfulness to his wife, virtuous children, her needs and maintenance for life — a burden. A man like that is not restrained by whether the woman is Muslim; if an idolatress makes marriage her condition, he will agree to it to meet his desire, without regard for the fact that such a bond has no validity in Islamic law. The second half of the ayah runs the same way for the woman: a truly believing man, for whom marriage is a religious trust, would not really want a woman who is a habitual adulterer and does not beg Allah's pardon, knowing she will not give up the habit after the marriage — so it is the adulterer whose aim is lust, or the idolater, who is drawn to her.

**An important limit.** The term "adulterer" is used here for men and women who do not repent and beg Allah's mercy, but stick to the habit. If a man with such a past marries a chaste woman for the sake of a household or of having children, this verse places no ban on that marriage; if such a woman marries a virtuous man intending a pure life, likewise. Such a marriage is valid under Islamic law — the view of the majority of jurists, including Imam Abu Hanifah, Imam Malik and Imam Shafiʿi — and it is established that Companions contracted such marriages. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr reports the same ruling from Ibn ʿAbbas.

**What "forbidden" forbids.** Some commentators read *dhālika* ("such a thing") as pointing back to zinā itself, which yields a sound meaning, though Maʿārif ul Qurʼān finds it far-fetched here; others read it as pointing to the marriages just described. It then distinguishes two senses of *ḥarām*. In the first, the act is a sin *and* has no legal validity in this world: if a Muslim man marries an idolatress or a woman of prohibited degree, the marriage itself is void. In the second, the act is forbidden and liable to punishment, but its legal consequences are recognised. A marriage contracted for some worldly expediency while the parties' real aim remains the sin falls in this second class — forbidden, yet legally recognised, so that maintenance, dower, proof of lineage and inheritance all apply. The prohibition has a concrete edge: a chaste man who marries such a woman and does not stop her from continuing after the marriage is doing something close to pimping, which is ḥarām — and the same holds for a chaste woman who lets her husband carry on. Read this way, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, there is no need to declare the verse cancelled, as some commentators did.

## Living it

Most readers will never sit as a judge. What this passage still asks of them is what the first verse named: *that you may remember*. Take seriously the safeguards this sūrah is about to legislate — the control of the gaze, the manners of entering houses — because the intent of the whole sūrah is to preserve chastity, even of the eyes. Feel pity for a wrongdoer — but never let pity set aside what Allah has fixed. And in marriage, remember that habits shape what a person can love: the door of repentance and of a clean new life is explicitly left open here, but a life not yet turned around tends to find its own likeness.

passages.title: Slandering chaste women and the door of repentance
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat protect a person's honour with the force of law. Ayah 4 lays down what happens to someone who accuses a chaste person of unlawful sexual intercourse and cannot produce four witnesses; ayah 5 opens a door of repentance for him. They belong together because the second is an exception clause attached to the first — the sentence is not finished until the mercy is spoken.

## Where this comes in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places this as **the third injunction relating to fornication** in this surah. The sequence matters. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, adultery is the most damaging and heinous of all crimes for society, and so its punishment under Islamic law is the most severe of all. But a law that punishes so heavily creates a new danger: the accusation itself becomes a weapon. A charge alone can destroy a person's life whether or not it is true.

So, in the words of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, justice and fairness required that special care be attached to proving this act, and that without the evidence prescribed by Islamic law no one should dare accuse any man or woman of adultery. Islamic law therefore made it mandatory to produce four honest, equitable, just men as witnesses to the crime; without them, the accusation is itself declared a grave crime, for which the prescribed punishment — the **ḥadd** — is eighty stripes. The accuser is not merely disbelieved. He is punished.

## The chilling effect is deliberate

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the practical logic. Under this rule, a man would only dare to make such an accusation if he were absolutely sure that he himself watched the act happen, **and** sure that three other honest men saw it too, **and** sure that they would actually give the evidence. If there are no other witnesses, or the total is fewer than four, or there is doubt whether the witnesses will testify, then no one would ever venture to give evidence alone and be punished with eighty stripes.

That is precisely the effect the commentary describes: the accusation is one that almost nobody will risk making without overwhelming certainty.

## "But then criminals go free" — and the answer

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious objection and answers it: if the conditions for proving adultery are this strong, will offenders not have a free hand, since no one will dare give evidence? The commentary calls this thinking totally wrong, and the reason turns on a distinction worth understanding.

- **Ḥadd** is the punishment fixed and prescribed by Islamic law — for zina, one hundred stripes or stoning.
- **Taʿzīr** is discretionary punishment, awarded by the judge or the ruler in accordance with the extent of the crime.

The four-witness condition is **exclusive to the ḥadd** for adultery. It does not shut down testimony generally. If a man and a woman who are not *maḥram* to one another — that is, not within the degrees of relationship that make marriage between them unlawful — are seen together in a compromising posture, or indulging in shameless acts, there is no restriction against giving evidence for that. All such matters connected to adultery are liable to punishment, awarded at the discretion of the judge or ruler, though not the maximum punishment of ḥadd. So someone who has seen the act but has no other witnesses need not give evidence of adultery itself; he can testify to having seen the accused in a compromising position, and the judge or ruler may award punishment once the crime is established.

The law is not naïve. It simply refuses to let a life be ruined on evidence that falls short.

## Who are the *muḥṣanāt*?

The ayah speaks of those who accuse *al-muḥṣanāt*. The word comes from **iḥṣān**, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — citing Jaṣṣāṣ — explains that Islamic jurisprudence recognises two types of iḥṣān, and it is easy to confuse them.

1. **Iḥṣān for the punishment of adultery.** Here it means the person against whom adultery is established is sane, adult, a free Muslim, validly married to a Muslim woman, and has consummated that marriage. In that case the punishment of stoning is awarded to him.
2. **Iḥṣān for the punishment of *qadhf*** — that is, for the offence of falsely accusing someone of adultery. Here it means the person against whom the charge is levelled is sane, adult, a free Muslim, and chaste, meaning he has not been proved an adulterer before.

**It is the second sense that the word carries in this ayah** (Jaṣṣāṣ). So the protected person is not "the married woman" but the *chaste* person — the one whose record is clean. Ibn Kathīr states the same: this ayah gives the prescribed punishment for making false accusations against chaste women, that is, those who are free, adult and chaste.

Two further clarifications follow from this:

- **Truth is a defence.** Ibn Kathīr: if the accuser produces evidence that what he is saying is true, then the punishment does not apply.
- **The gender of the ayah is illustrative, not restrictive.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the ayah describes the accusers as men and the accused as a chaste lady, either because of general practice or because of the incident for which the verse was revealed. But the injunction applies to all situations, on the common ground applicable to all persons: if a woman levels a charge of adultery against another woman or against a man, or a man accuses another man, and the required legal evidence is lacking, then in either case the accuser is liable to eighty stripes (Jaṣṣāṣ, Hidāyah). Ibn Kathīr says the same in one line: if the person falsely accused is a man, the same punishment of flogging also applies.

## Three consequences, not one

Ibn Kathīr sets out the structure of ayah 4 with great clarity. If the accuser cannot prove that what he is saying is true, **three rulings** apply to him:

1. **He is flogged with eighty stripes.**
2. **His testimony is rejected forever.**
3. **He is labelled a *fāsiq*** — a rebellious person who is not of good character, "whether in the sight of Allah or of mankind."

Notice the shape of it. The first falls on the body. The second falls on his standing in the community: a man whose word is no longer received in any matter has lost something he cannot buy back. The third, in Ibn Kathīr's own words, touches how he stands both before Allah and before people. The accusation was aimed at another person's good name; the consequences settle on the accuser's own.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the same point in two parts: one punishment is inflicted at once — the eighty stripes — and another stays with the culprit forever, namely that his evidence will not be accepted in any matter.

## This is the accused person's right

One ruling in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān deserves to be sat with. The punishment prescribed for **qadhf** relates to the *right of the person against whom the charge was levelled*. It is executed only when that person demands its execution; otherwise it is annulled. This is unlike the punishment for adultery, which is purely a right of Allah, and therefore has to be executed even if no one has ever demanded it.

That single distinction tells you what these ayat are protecting. The ḥadd for zina defends an order that Allah has laid down. The ḥadd for qadhf defends *a human being's honour* — and so it is placed in that human being's hands. If the wronged person chooses to let it go, it drops.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes, citing Jaṣṣāṣ and Hidāyah, that the eighty stripes as ḥadd are **exclusive to false accusation of adultery** and do not apply to the accusation of any other crime. False accusations of other crimes can be punished, but by taʿzīr. The Qur'an does not state that exclusiveness in so many words; the proof of it is the four-witness condition itself, since four witnesses are required only in the case of adultery.

## Ayah 5: the exception

> **"Except those who repent afterwards and mend their ways; then, Allah is All-Forgiving, Very-Merciful."**

Repentance here is not a word said and forgotten. The ayah pairs *tāba* (repented) with *aṣlaḥū* — Ibn Kathīr renders it "and do righteous deeds," Maʿārif ul Qurʼān "mend their ways." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells out the standard being asked for: those punished for false accusation, if they beg pardon and improve their habits **so that there is no risk of the falsehood being repeated**, and also obtain forgiveness from the one they had accused, then Allah grants forgiveness and is Merciful. A slandered reputation is a debt owed to a person as well as a sin against Allah; the tongue that caused the wound is asked to go back and seek pardon from the one it wounded.

And then the closing words: **Allah is Ghafūr, Raḥīm** — Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful. After a passage of stripes and disqualification and the label *fāsiq*, the last thing the reader is left holding is two of Allah's names. Even the slanderer is not written off.

## What exactly does the exception cover? The scholars differ

This is where the sources genuinely disagree, and it would be dishonest to flatten it. The question is: which of the three consequences does "except those who repent" reach?

**Agreed by all:** the flogging is carried out regardless of whether he repents or persists, and after that there is no further punishment for it — Ibn Kathīr says this is agreed among the scholars. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise reports that all scholars are unanimous that **repentance does not remit a ḥadd punishment**; what is pardoned by repentance is the torment of the Hereafter.

**The first view — the exception reaches the second and third consequences.** Ibn Kathīr holds that the exception refers to the second and third rulings: if he repents, his testimony may be accepted, and he is no longer to be regarded as rebellious. He attributes this to **Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib — "the leader of the Tābiʿīn"** — and also a group among the Salaf. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports a parallel position from **Imām al-Shāfiʿī** and some other Imams: they take the exception to govern all the sentences of the previous ayah, which means that since he does not remain a sinner after repentance, he is also not debarred from giving evidence.

**A refinement.** Ibn Kathīr records that **al-Shaʿbī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk** said his testimony cannot be accepted even if he repents — *unless he himself admits that he said something false*, in which case his testimony may be accepted. Ibn Kathīr closes that discussion with "And Allah knows best."

**The second view — the exception reaches only the label.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that according to **Imām Abū Ḥanīfah** and some other Imams, the exception refers only to the last sentence of ayah 4, *"and those are the rebellious."* On this reading, the one punished for false accusation is a sinner; but if he repents with sincerity and improves himself after obtaining forgiveness from the one he falsely accused, he no longer remains a sinner and his punishment in the Hereafter is pardoned. The two worldly punishments named at the beginning of the ayah — the eighty stripes and the inadmissibility of his evidence — remain despite the repentance. The reasoning: the punishment of stripes has already been executed, and the second punishment is **itself part of the ḥadd**; since all agree that repentance does not remit a ḥadd, the inadmissibility of his evidence is not remitted either.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note of consensus and a note of difference in the same breath: that his evidence is not accepted unless he begs Allah's pardon with sincere repentance and is also forgiven by the one he had accused is by consensus of the Ummah; but in the Ḥanafī position, even after begging that pardon his evidence is not acceptable — **only his sin is pardoned.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that Jaṣṣāṣ and Maẓharī have provided the arguments on both sides, and that those interested may consult them. It is enough for the reader here to hold both views with respect: this is a genuine difference among the Imams over the reach of one Arabic exception particle, not a case of one side neglecting the text.

## Living it

- **Weigh what an accusation costs.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that these eighty stripes as ḥadd are exclusive to the false accusation of adultery and do not apply to the accusation of any other crime; other false accusations are punishable by taʿzīr instead. Allah has fenced a person's sexual honour with a protection unlike any other — and He fenced it against *us*, against our mouths.
- **"I heard" is not evidence.** Under this ayah, even someone who has seen the act but lacks three other witnesses need not give evidence of the act itself. How much more so someone repeating a rumour they did not see.
- **Suspicion has a lawful outlet, and it is not gossip.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's answer to the doubt shows the way: what is seen short of the act can be testified to before the judge or ruler, who may award punishment at his discretion once the crime is established. What it may never become is talk.
- **The wound is owed to a person.** Because the ḥadd for qadhf relates to the right of the one accused, and because the repentance described in ayah 5 involves obtaining that person's forgiveness, whoever has damaged someone's name has business with them, not only with Allah.
- **And no one is beyond return.** Ayah 5 is placed exactly where a reader might assume a case is closed. The passage that names a man *fāsiq* ends by naming Allah *Ghafūr, Raḥīm*.

passages.title: Li'ān: the husband's four oaths and the fifth
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat open a door that ayah 4 had closed. There, anyone who accuses a chaste woman of adultery and cannot produce four witnesses is himself flogged eighty stripes and his testimony is rejected forever. But what about a husband — a man who has seen it with his own eyes, in his own house? Ayat 6 and 7 give him, and only him, a way through: four solemn testimonies sworn by Allah that he is telling the truth, and a fifth in which he calls down Allah's curse on himself if he is lying.

## The word itself: liʿān

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that **liʿān** comes from the sense of cursing — its meaning, it says, "is to curse and praying for Allah's wrath on each other." In Islamic law the name is given to certain specific oaths sworn between a husband and wife, each of them invoking Allah's condemnation upon whichever of the two is lying.

Ayah 6 does not simply say he swears; it says **his testimony shall be four testimonies by Allah** — the Arabic word is *shahādāt*, testimonies, the same kind of word used for the evidence of witnesses in a court. And the ayah's own condition is that he has "no witnesses except themselves." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that under 24:4 an accuser must produce four eyewitnesses, "one of them he being himself." Here, where those four are impossible, the ayah lets his own repeated testimony carry the case.

## Why a husband is a special case

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the difficulty plainly. An ordinary man who suspects something but cannot bring four eyewitnesses can simply stay silent and protect himself from the eighty stripes. The husband is trapped: "if he accuses his wife without the support of four eye-witnesses he will be liable to punishment of eighty stripes, and if he keeps quiet, it will be a lifelong agony for him to live with the knowledge that his wife has been unfaithful to him." So, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "the husband's case has been separated from the general law and a separate provision has been prescribed, which is exclusive to the case between husband and wife." For everyone else the ruling of the preceding ayat stands unchanged.

Ibn Kathir reads the passage the same way: **"This Ayah offers a way out for husbands."** It is not primarily a licence to accuse. It is a release for a man otherwise crushed between two impossible options.

Ibn Kathir also records, from Imam Ahmad, a report of Saʿīd bin Jubayr in which Ibn ʿUmar described the very first man to raise this question. He asked the Prophet ﷺ about a man who sees his wife committing an immoral sin: "If he speaks he will be speaking about something very serious, and if he keeps quiet he will be keeping quiet about something very serious." The Prophet ﷺ kept quiet and gave him no answer. Later the man came back and said that the thing he had asked about was something he was now being tested with himself. That report was recorded, Ibn Kathir notes, by An-Nasāʼi in his Tafsir and by Al-Bukhari and Muslim in the Two Sahihs.

## The night that produced these ayat

Ibn Kathir gives the story at length, from a report Imam Ahmad recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās. When the ayah of the eighty stripes (24:4) was revealed, Saʿd bin ʿUbādah — the leader of the Ansār — said, "Is this how it was revealed, O Messenger of Allah?" The Prophet ﷺ turned to his people: **"O Ansār, did you hear what your leader said?"** They rushed to defend him: "do not blame him, for he is a jealous man." They described a man of such fierce protectiveness that he never married a woman who was not a virgin, and that when he divorced a woman none of them would dare to marry her.

Then Saʿd explained himself: "By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, I know that it is true and is from Allah, but I am surprised. If I found some wicked man lying down with my wife, should I not disturb him until I have brought four witnesses? By Allah, he would have finished what he was doing before I could bring them!"

A little while later the hypothetical became real. Hilāl bin Umayyah — whom Ibn Kathir identifies as one of the three whose repentance had been accepted — came back from his lands at night and found a man with his wife. He saw with his own eyes and heard with his own ears. And **he did not disturb him.** He waited until morning and took it to the Prophet ﷺ.

The Prophet ﷺ, we are told, did not like what he had said and got very upset. In the version Al-Bukhari narrates from Ibn ʿAbbās — where the man named is Sharīk bin Sahmāʼ — he said to Hilāl: **"Evidence, or the punishment on your back."** Hilāl protested — "O Messenger of Allah, if any one of us saw a man with his wife, how could he go and get evidence?" — and the Prophet ﷺ repeated it: **"Evidence, otherwise the punishment on your back."** The Ansār gathered around, saying to one another that the very thing Saʿd had warned of had come to pass, and Hilāl would now be flogged and his testimony declared unacceptable before the people.

Hilāl answered: "By Allah, I hope that Allah will make for me a way out from this problem." In Al-Bukhari's version: "By the One Who sent you with the truth! I am telling the truth and Allah will reveal something that will protect my back from the punishment."

Ibn Kathir's report says the Prophet ﷺ wanted to have him flogged — and then the revelation came. They knew it from the change in his face, and they would leave him alone until the revelation was finished. Then he said: **"Rejoice, O Hilāl, for Allah has made a way out for you."** Hilāl replied, "I had been hoping for this from my Lord, may He be glorified."

## What happened in that room

The Prophet ﷺ said, **"Send for her."** She came. He recited the ayah to them both and reminded them that the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe than the punishment in this world. Hilāl said, "By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, I have spoken the truth about her." She said, "He is lying."

Then: **"Make them both swear the liʿān."**

Hilāl was told, "Testify," and he testified four times by Allah that he was one of those who speak the truth. Before the fifth he was warned: "O Hilāl, have Taqwa of Allah" — that is, fear Him and be mindful of Him — "for the punishment of this world is easier than the punishment of the Hereafter, and this will mean that the punishment will be inevitable for you." He answered, "By Allah, Allah will not punish me for it, just as He has not caused me to be flogged for it" — and testified the fifth time that Allah's curse be upon him if he was telling a lie.

Then his wife was told to testify four times by Allah that he was telling a lie. At the fifth she was given the same warning. In this report she hesitated for a while and was about to admit her guilt, then said, "By Allah, I will not expose my people to shame," and swore the fifth oath. She chose her family's reputation over her own soul, in front of everyone, at the very edge of confession.

Al-Bukhari's version preserves two further moments. There, after Hilāl had given his testimony and before she gave hers, the Prophet ﷺ said: **"Allah knows that one of you is lying. Will one of you repent?"** And when she reached her fifth oath, they stopped her and said, "If you swear the fifth oath and you are lying, the curse of Allah will be inevitable." Ibn ʿAbbās's words in that version are: **"She hesitated and kept quiet until we thought that she had changed her mind"** — then she said, "I will not dishonour my people today," and she went ahead. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, telling the story from Tafsir Mazhari on the authority of Musnad Ahmad from Ibn ʿAbbās, places a similar appeal earlier still: when she denied the accusation, the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah knows one of the two of them is a liar, and asked would they not dread Allah's torment, come out with the truth and repent.)

The Prophet ﷺ then separated them. He decreed that her child should not be attributed to any father, nor should the child be accused, and that whoever accused her or her child would be subject to punishment. He also decreed that Hilāl was not obliged to house her or feed her, because they had not been separated by divorce, nor had he died and left her a widow. He then described in advance what the child would look like if it were Hilāl's and what it would look like if it belonged to the man she was accused with; the child was born matching the second description, and the Prophet ﷺ said, **"Were it not for the oath that she swore, I would deal with her"** — in Al-Bukhari's wording, **"Were it not for the Book of Allah, I would deal with her."** ʿIkrimah adds that the child grew up to become the governor of Egypt, given his mother's name and attributed to no father.

The sign was there in front of everyone in the room. And still the law held, because Allah had made the sworn oath — not suspicion, not resemblance — the thing that decides the case in this world.

## Two incidents, one law

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the books of Hadith record two incidents on this subject, and that the commentators differ over which was the occasion of revelation. The second is narrated in the Sahihs on the authority of Sahl bin Saʿd al-Sāʿidī: ʿUwaimir al-ʿAjlānī asked the Prophet ﷺ what a man should do who finds his wife in bed with another man — should he kill him and be killed by the people in return, or what else? The Prophet ﷺ answered that Allah had revealed an injunction for the case of him and his wife, and told him to go and bring her; the liʿān was performed in the mosque. When it was done ʿUwaimir said, "If I still keep her as my wife this will mean as if I had made a false accusation against her" — and pronounced divorce. Baghawi's fuller account, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās, sets this up with ʿĀsim bin ʿAdiyy raising Saʿd's same objection from the crowd on a Friday, only for the case to strike his own family within the week.

**Where the scholars stood:** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that Qurtubi took both incidents as causes of revelation, the revelation having come down twice. It then gives the explanation of Hafiz Ibn Hajar (the annotator of Al-Bukhari) and Nawawi (the annotator of Muslim), whose reasoning it calls "more appealing": that the first incident was Hilāl bin Umayyah's, and the ayat of liʿān were revealed in connection with it; immediately afterwards ʿUwaimir was confronted with a similar case, perhaps not knowing what had already happened, and the Prophet ﷺ simply told him the judgment in his case. The evidence is in the wording of the two reports: for Hilāl it is *"then Jibrāʼīl descended"* with the ayat; for ʿUwaimir it is *"Allah has revealed about you"* — which can mean that Allah has already enjoined His command in a case similar to yours. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.

## The fifth oath (ayah 7)

Ayah 7 requires him to add: **"and a fifth oath that Allah may condemn him if he is lying."** He must pronounce the curse on his own head.

He is not merely alleging something about her; he is putting his own standing with his Lord on the table. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the Prophet ﷺ stopped Hilāl at exactly this point, warning him to be careful and fear Allah, "as worldly punishment is lighter than the torment of the Hereafter. The torment of Allah is much more severe than the punishment of people, and that the fifth testimony is the final one, on which the ruling would depend." Eighty stripes hurt for a season; Allah's curse is another order of thing entirely. A liar is being offered one last exit before the door shuts. The same pause was given to the wife.

Reading on into the ayat that follow, Ibn Kathir notes the difference in what she invokes: *ghadab*, Allah's wrath, rather than *laʿnah*, His curse. His explanation: "usually a man would not go to the extent of exposing his wife and accusing her of Zina unless he is telling the truth and has good reason to do this, and she knows that what he is accusing her of is true. So in her case the fifth testimony calls for the wrath of Allah to be upon her, for the one upon whom is the wrath of Allah, is the one who knows the truth yet deviates from it."

## How the procedure works

From Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the sequence is: a husband accuses his wife of adultery (or refuses to own her child as his); she rejects the allegation as false and claims the eighty stripes for false accusation against him; the husband is asked to produce four witnesses. If he produces them, the punishment for adultery falls on her. If he cannot, the two are subjected to liʿān — first his four testimonies and his fifth self-curse, then hers.

Refusal is not an option that quietly ends the matter. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that if the husband hesitates to say the words he is arrested and not released until he either swears the five times or accepts that he is a liar — and if he accepts that, the prescribed punishment for false accusation of adultery (*hadd al-qadhf*) is applied to him. If the wife then refuses to swear, she likewise is held until she either swears the five times or accepts her guilt, in which case the punishment for adultery is applied to her. If both complete the five, the process is complete, both escape punishment in this world, and — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it — in the Hereafter the one who has lied will suffer, "as Allah knows best who is the liar."

Ibn Kathir describes the same act as taking place before the Imam, the husband stating his accusation and the ruler asking him to swear four times by Allah in front of four witnesses. On the effect of the husband's oaths he says that once he has spoken them **"she is divorced from him by the very act of this Liʿan; she is forever forbidden for him and he must give her Mahr to her"** — the Mahr being the marriage payment owed to a wife — and that nothing can prevent the prescribed punishment from falling on her except her own oaths in reply. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, giving the ruling of Imam Abu Hanifah, holds that the unlawfulness is established immediately upon the liʿān, but that the husband should then free the woman by divorcing her; if he does not, the ruler or judge orders the separation, which has the same force as divorce, after which she completes three menstrual cycles and is then free to marry another man. (The waiting period before remarriage — the *ʿiddah* — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives here as three months, that is, three cycles.)

**Three settled consequences,** as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists them:

- The couple are forbidden to each other permanently — likened to the way foster relatives are forbidden to marry one another forever. The Prophet ﷺ said that the spouses who have gone through liʿān can never come together again.
- The child conceived is not called by the husband's name but by the mother's. The Prophet ﷺ gave this ruling in both the case of Hilāl bin Umayyah and that of ʿUwaimir al-ʿAjlānī.
- The woman may not be called an adulteress, nor her child illegitimate; the punishment of this world is annulled for both, however the burden of the Hereafter falls on whichever of them lied. The Prophet ﷺ ruled precisely this in Hilāl's case.

## Living with these ayat

Ibn Kathir reads on to ayah 10 to name what all of this is: **"had it not been for the grace of Allah and His mercy on you"** — meaning, in his words, that without it "many of your affairs would have been too difficult for you." That is the register in which to read ayat 6 and 7. This is a mercy, and it looks like one only if you first feel the impossibility it answers.

Three things this passage asks of a believer.

**Take oaths by Allah with the seriousness the Prophet ﷺ showed.** He stopped the proceedings twice — once for Hilāl, once for his wife — to say that the punishment of this world is easier than the punishment of the Hereafter. If a man will interrupt a legal process to save a liar from his own tongue, the casual oath in ordinary conversation deserves a second thought.

**Notice what Allah protects even in the wreckage.** The marriage is over and one of the two is certainly lying, yet the ruling still shields the woman's name and the child's honour, and threatens punishment on anyone who accuses either of them. The community is not given permission to finish what the courtroom left unresolved.

**And notice Hilāl.** He had every reason to despair — the ruling was against him, the Prophet ﷺ was upset, the flogging was moments away — and he said he hoped Allah would make a way out for him. Ibn Kathir also notes that ayah 10 calls Allah *Tawwāb*, the One who forgives and accepts repentance — and comments that this is from His servants "even if that comes after they have sworn a confirmed oath." The door of repentance is not sealed even for the one who swore falsely with Allah's curse on his own head. Allah is also *Hakīm*, the All-Wise — as Ibn Kathir says, "in what He prescribes and commands and forbids." The wisdom is in the whole design: a law that refuses to convict on suspicion, refuses to leave a wronged husband voiceless, and leaves the final verdict where it always belonged, with the One who knows best which of the two was lying.

These three ayat finish the escape route that opened in ayat 6–7. There, a husband who accuses his wife of adultery but has no witnesses beyond himself is told to swear four times by Allah that he is truthful, and a fifth time to call down Allah's curse upon himself if he is lying. Now the Qur'an turns to the wife. Ayah 8 gives her the matching right — her own four oaths — and ayah 9 her fifth, invoking Allah's wrath upon herself if her husband is truthful. Ayah 10 then steps back from the whole grim procedure and names it: grace, mercy, forgiveness, wisdom. That is what holds the passage together — a marriage in ruins, two people swearing against each other before Allah, and the Qur'an insisting that the very existence of this way out is a kindness.

This procedure is called **li'ān** (لِعَان). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word plainly: it comes from *cursing*, and means the two of them cursing and praying for Allah's wrath upon each other. In Islamic law it is the name given to this specific kind of oath sworn between a husband and wife.

## The objection that made a leader of the Ansār speak up

Ibn Kathir says there are hadiths explaining how this ayah is put into effect, why it was revealed, and about whom. The story begins one ayah earlier in the surah.

Imam Ahmad recorded from Ibn 'Abbas that when ayah 4 came down — that anyone who accuses a chaste woman and cannot produce four witnesses is to be flogged eighty lashes and never accepted as a witness again — Sa'd bin 'Ubadah, the leader of the Ansār, said, "Is this how it was revealed, O Messenger of Allah?" The Prophet ﷺ said to the people: **"O Ansār, did you hear what your leader said?"** They pleaded for him: do not blame him, he is a jealous man; he never married a woman who was not a virgin, and never divorced one whom any of us would then dare to marry, so fierce is his sense of honour.

Sa'd then spoke for himself. He was not doubting the revelation — "I know that it is true and is from Allah" — but he was staggered by it. If he found some wicked man lying with his wife, was he really to leave the man undisturbed and go looking for four witnesses? "By Allah, he would have finished what he was doing before I could bring them!"

That is the human pressure behind this passage, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the logic of it. An ordinary person who suspects something and cannot prove it can simply stay silent and be safe. A husband cannot. If he speaks without four witnesses he takes eighty lashes; if he stays silent he lives a lifetime with what he saw. So the husband's case was lifted out of the general law of accusation and given its own provision, exclusive to the case between husband and wife. For everyone else, the directive of the preceding ayat still stands.

## Hilāl bin Umayyah's night

Not long after Sa'd's protest, the thing itself happened. Ibn Kathir continues the narration from Imam Ahmad: Hilāl bin Umayyah — one of the three whose repentance Allah accepted — came back from his fields at night and found a man with his wife. He saw with his own eyes and heard with his own ears. And he did not disturb him until morning.

In the morning he told the Prophet ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ did not like what he heard and was deeply upset. The Ansār gathered, saying to one another that the very thing Sa'd had raised was now upon them, and that Hilāl would be flogged and his testimony rejected for life. Hilāl said, "By Allah, I hope that Allah will make for me a way out from this problem." He said to the Prophet ﷺ, "I see how upset you are by what I have said, but Allah knows that I am telling the truth."

In the version Al-Bukhari records from Ibn 'Abbas, the exchange is starker still. The Prophet ﷺ told him: **"Evidence, or the punishment on your back."** Hilāl asked how a man who sees another with his wife could possibly go and fetch evidence. The Prophet ﷺ repeated: **"Evidence, otherwise the punishment on your back."** Hilāl answered, "By the One Who sent you with the truth! I am telling the truth and Allah will reveal something that will protect my back from the punishment."

Then the revelation came. Those present knew it from the change in the Prophet's face; they would leave him alone until it finished. When it ended he said, **"Rejoice, O Hilāl, for Allah has made a way out for you."** Hilāl replied, "I had been hoping for this from my Lord, may He be glorified."

Notice what Hilāl's hope was made of. He did not appeal to his rank, or argue the law, or take matters into his own hands. He waited until morning, and then he waited for Allah — and ayat 6–9 are the answer.

## The oath-taking itself

**"Send for her,"** the Prophet ﷺ said. When both stood before him, he recited the ayah to them and reminded them that the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe than the punishment of this world — the sentence Ibn Kathir singles out as the heart of this scene. In the Bukhari version he put it to them directly: **"Allah knows that one of you is lying. Will one of you repent?"**

Hilāl said, "By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, I have spoken the truth about her." She said, "He is lying." So he said: **"Make them both swear the li'ān."**

Hilāl testified four times by Allah that he was truthful. At the fifth he was stopped and warned: have taqwā of Allah — mindful fear of Him — for the punishment of this world is easier than the punishment of the Hereafter, and this oath makes the punishment inevitable for you. He answered, "By Allah, Allah will not punish me for it, just as He has not caused me to be flogged for it" — and swore that Allah's curse be upon him if he lied.

Then his wife was told to testify. She swore four times that he was lying. At the fifth she was warned in the same words. In Imam Ahmad's narration she hesitated for a while and was about to admit her guilt, then said, "By Allah, I will not expose my people to shame." In Al-Bukhari's version Ibn 'Abbas, who was watching, said she hesitated and kept quiet so long that they thought she had changed her mind, and then said: **"I will not dishonour my people today."** She swore the fifth oath, that the wrath of Allah be upon her if he was telling the truth.

The Prophet ﷺ separated them. It is worth sitting with that pause of hers. Ayah 9 is not a formality; it is a moment in which a human being stands at the edge of the Hereafter and chooses. Nothing in the text tells us which of the two lied. That is precisely the point of the procedure: the courtroom closes, and the case is left with Allah.

## "She averts the punishment" — the wording of ayah 8

Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase exactly: **"But she shall avert the punishment"** means *the prescribed punishment* — the fixed penalty for zinā that would otherwise fall on her once her husband has completed his oaths.

Ibn Kathir is precise about the sequence. Once the husband has sworn his five oaths, she is divorced from him by that very act of li'ān, she is forever forbidden to him, and he must give her her *mahr* (dower). At that point the punishment for zinā stands against her, "and nothing can prevent the punishment except if she also swears the oath of condemnation."

So her oaths are not a courtesy. In this passage they are her shield, and the Qur'an gives her exactly the weight it gave him — four oaths against four, a fifth against a fifth. Against a husband's sworn word, hers alone is enough to hold the punishment off.

## Curse for him, wrath for her — ayah 9

The one point of wording the commentary dwells on is why ayah 7 calls down *la'nah* (curse) on the lying husband while ayah 9 calls down *ghaḍab* (wrath) on the wife.

Ibn Kathir's answer: the wrath of Allah is mentioned specially in the case of the woman because a man would not normally go so far as to expose his own wife and accuse her of zinā unless he were telling the truth and had good reason — and if he is, then she knows perfectly well that the accusation is true. Her denial would be a lie told in full knowledge. And he adds the principle that ties the word to the case: **the one upon whom is the wrath of Allah is the one who knows the truth yet deviates from it.**

What the fifth oath does, then, is put a person's own standing before Allah on the line. That is exactly why the Prophet ﷺ halted both of them before it and reminded each one that the punishment of this world is easier than the punishment of the Hereafter.

## Two incidents, one law

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports a second incident, quoted in the Ṣaḥīḥs of Bukhari and Muslim, with the details narrated by Baghawī on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas. The Prophet ﷺ was on the minbar reciting ayah 4 when 'Āṣim bin 'Adiyy al-Anṣārī rose and asked the same question Sa'd had asked: if a man finds his wife with another man and reports it, he is flogged eighty times, barred from testimony for life, and called a liar by the Muslims — how is he to get eyewitnesses on the spot, when by the time he fetches them the man will have gone? This was on a Friday. Then 'Āṣim's own cousin 'Uwaimir found his wife with Sharīk bin Saḥmā'; 'Āṣim, on hearing it, said *innā lillāhi wa innā ilayhi rājiʿūn* and went to the Prophet ﷺ the following day — again a Friday — to say that the question he had asked had now landed in his own family.

In the version from Sahl bin Sa'd as-Sā'idī in the Ṣaḥīḥs, 'Uwaimir al-'Ajlānī asked whether a man in that situation should kill the other man and be killed for it, or what else he should do. The Prophet ﷺ told him Allah had revealed a ruling concerning him and his wife, and had them perform the li'ān in the mosque. When it was done, 'Uwaimir said that if he kept her it would look as though he had lied about her, and pronounced three divorces.

So which incident occasioned the revelation? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the commentators differ. Qurṭubī took both as causes of revelation, the revelation having come twice. Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Ḥajar, the commentator on Bukhari, and Imam Nawawī, the commentator on Muslim, reconciled them: the verses came down for Hilāl's case first, and 'Uwaimir — perhaps not knowing what had just happened — brought a near-identical case immediately after and was given the ruling. Their evidence is a difference in wording: in Hilāl's report, "then Jibrīl descended with these verses," whereas in 'Uwaimir's, "Allah has revealed about you," which can mean that Allah had already legislated for a case like his. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān finds their reasoning more appealing, and closes the matter as such matters should be closed: *wallāhu subḥānahu wa taʿālā aʿlam*.

## What the ruling looks like in practice

Ibn Kathir describes the shape of it: the husband brings her before the Imam and states the accusation; the ruler has him swear the four oaths and then the fifth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the surrounding law:

- If the husband cannot produce four witnesses, husband and wife are put to li'ān. If he **refuses** to swear, he is detained until he either swears or admits he lied — and if he admits it, he receives the fixed penalty for false accusation of adultery (*ḥadd al-qadhf*). If she refuses to swear, she is likewise detained until she swears or confesses her guilt.
- Once both have sworn, **the worldly punishment falls away from both**. The one who lied still faces it in the Hereafter, "as Allah knows best who is the liar."
- The couple are **forbidden to each other permanently**, once li'ān has taken place before the judge. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likens it to the permanence of foster-relation prohibitions, and cites the Prophet's ﷺ words that two who have gone through li'ān can never come together again. As for her remarrying another man: if the husband releases her by divorce, or states that he has left her, she may remarry after the expiry of her waiting period (*'iddah*) of three months — this being the ruling of Imam Abū Ḥanīfah. If he does neither, the ruler or the judge orders the separation, which has the same force as a divorce, and after that she completes three menstrual periods and is then free to marry another man.
- The **child** conceived is called after the mother and not attributed to the husband. The Prophet ﷺ gave this ruling in both cases, Hilāl's and 'Uwaimir's.
- And the protection that follows is remarkable: it is **not permitted to call the woman an adulteress, nor to call her child illegitimate**. Ibn Kathir's narration says the Prophet ﷺ decreed that her child should not be attributed to any father, nor should the child be accused, and that whoever accused her or her child would himself be subject to punishment. 'Ikrimah reports that this child grew up to become the governor of Egypt, known by his mother's name.

Ibn Kathir also notes that Hilāl was not obliged to house or feed her, since they had not been separated by divorce, nor had he died and left her a widow.

One further scene the reports preserve makes the force of ayah 8 unmistakable. The Prophet ﷺ said that if she gave birth to a child of one description the child was Hilāl's, and if of another, it was the child of the man she had been accused with. The child was born matching the second description — and he said, **"Were it not for the oath that she swore, I would deal with her,"** in Bukhari's wording, **"Were it not for the Book of Allah, I would deal with her."** The Prophet ﷺ, with every human indication before him, still would not punish her. Her oaths had done exactly what ayah 8 says they do. Once a person invokes Allah against herself in the form Allah prescribed, the matter passes out of human hands.

## Ayah 10: naming the whole thing mercy

After all of that — the accusation, the oaths, the curse, the wrath, the shattered marriage — ayah 10 says: **"And had it not been for the grace of Allah and His mercy on you!"** The sentence is deliberately left hanging, its consequence unstated. Ibn Kathir supplies it: many of your affairs would have been too difficult for you. Here, he says, Allah is mentioning His grace and kindness to His creation in that He has prescribed for them a way out of their difficulties.

Then Allah names Himself **Tawwāb**, the One who forgives and accepts repentance — and Ibn Kathir presses the point exactly where it is hardest to believe: He accepts repentance from His servants *even after they have sworn a confirmed oath*. Ayah 10 is aimed straight at whichever of the two lied under oath and walked away uncondemned in this world. The door is not shut on him or her. And **Ḥakīm**, the All-Wise, Ibn Kathir says, in what He prescribes and commands and forbids — so this whole uncomfortable procedure is wisdom, not compromise.

## Living it

**Wait for Allah's way out rather than seizing your own.** Sa'd asked his question and accepted the answer. Hilāl saw the worst a man can see, waited until morning, then waited for revelation. 'Uwaimir asked whether to kill, and was told there was a lawful path instead. Each of them was given something better than what he would have done in the heat of the moment.

**Do not swear lightly by Allah.** Twice in these narrations the Prophet ﷺ halted a person at the fifth oath to say the same thing: the punishment of this world is easier than the punishment of the Hereafter. An oath by Allah is not a rhetorical flourish.

**Guard the innocent who stand near the guilty.** The most striking rulings here protect a woman no court cleared and a child whose paternity was never established: she may not be called an adulteress, he may not be called illegitimate, and anyone who accuses either of them is himself subject to punishment. And that child grew up to govern Egypt.

**Leave to Allah what only Allah can settle.** After li'ān, one of the two is certainly lying and no one on earth knows which. The Qur'an closes the case in this world and hands it to the One who forgives, accepts repentance, and is All-Wise in everything He legislates.

passages.title: The slander of 'Ā'ishah and the believers' failure
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat are Allah's answer to a lie: a slander invented against 'A'ishah, wife of the Prophet ﷺ and Mother of the believers, which circulated in Madinah for about a month until Allah sent down her innocence from heaven. The passage does two things at once — it clears her name, and it puts the believing community on trial for how it handled a rumour.

Ma'arif ul Qur'an places these ayat where the surah has been heading: an-Nur has been legislating the protection of chastity — the hadd for zina, then the hadd for false accusation (qadhf: eighty lashes for accusing a chaste woman without four eyewitnesses), then li'an. Here Allah Himself takes up her defence — revealing, as Ibn Kathir notes, ten ayat concerning her.

## The story behind the ayat

Ibn Kathir records the account through Imam Ahmad from az-Zuhri, who gathered it from four men — among them Sa'id bin al-Musayyib and 'Urwah bin az-Zubayr — each of whom heard it from 'A'ishah herself; al-Bukhari and Muslim both recorded it in their Sahihs from the hadith of az-Zuhri. Ma'arif ul Qur'an identifies the campaign as the expedition against Banu al-Mustaliq (Muraysi'), in the sixth year after the Hijrah.

When the Prophet ﷺ travelled he would draw lots among his wives; 'A'ishah's lot came out. This was after the command of hijab, so she travelled inside a covered howdah lifted onto the camel. Returning, as they approached Madinah, the army halted and then announced departure. She had stepped away to relieve herself and noticed her necklace had broken, so she went back to search. Meanwhile the men lifted her howdah onto the camel assuming she was inside. She found the necklace, came back, and the army was gone. She sat down where the caravan had been and fell asleep, reasoning — as Ma'arif ul Qur'an notes — that the Prophet ﷺ would send men back for her, and that wandering off would only make the search harder.

Safwan bin al-Mu'attal, assigned to travel at the rear, reached the place at dawn. He recognised her, having seen her before hijab was made obligatory, and said only, "Truly, to Allah we belong, and truly, to Him we shall return." She woke and covered her face with her jilbab. By her own testimony he did not speak a word to her beyond that phrase. He made his camel kneel, she rode, and he led it on foot until they reached the army at Zuhr time.

Out of that — a woman riding openly into the whole army at midday — 'Abdullah bin Ubayy bin Salul, head of the hypocrites, manufactured a filthy accusation, dragging Safwan's honour through the mud alongside hers. Some Muslims began to believe it; others thought it possible and repeated it.

## A month of silence

Back in Madinah 'A'ishah fell ill for a month, knowing nothing of what was being said. What wounded her was that the Prophet's ﷺ usual kindness was absent; he would come in, say only "How is that lady?", and leave.

Going out at night with Umm Mistah, her companion stumbled and cursed her own son, Mistah. 'A'ishah rebuked her: how can you abuse a man who was present at Badr? "Have you not heard what he said?" — and out came the whole story. Her illness doubled. She asked permission to go to her parents. "Subhan Allah! Are the people really talking about that?" She wept the whole night without sleeping.

The Prophet ﷺ, grieved and receiving no revelation, called 'Ali bin Abi Talib and Usamah bin Zayd and consulted them. Usamah spoke plainly for her: she is your wife, and we know nothing about her but good. 'Ali said that Allah had not imposed restrictions on him and there were plenty of other women.

Then the Prophet ﷺ stood on the minbar: "O Muslims, who will help me against a man who has hurt me by slandering my family? By Allah, I know nothing about my family but good, and the people are blaming a man of whom I know nothing except good, and he has never entered upon my family except with me." The appeal nearly set al-Aws and al-Khazraj at each other's throats until the Prophet ﷺ calmed them down.

## "If you are innocent, Allah will declare it"

Finally the Prophet ﷺ came in and sat with her — the first time since the rumours began — recited the Tashahhud, and said: "Thereafter, O 'A'ishah, I have been told such and such a thing about you. If you are innocent, then Allah will reveal your innocence; but if you have committed a sin, then seek Allah's forgiveness and turn in repentance to Him, for when a servant confesses his sin and repents to Allah, He accepts his repentance."

Her tears stopped dead. She asked her father to answer for him; he said he did not know what to say. She asked her mother; the same. So this young woman who, by her own admission, had not memorised much of the Qur'an, spoke — and Ma'arif ul Qur'an observes that in such distress even extremely learned and intelligent people would have struggled to express themselves in a balanced way, yet what she said was a piece of highly intellectual and scholarly discourse:

"By Allah, I know that you have heard so much of this story that it has become planted in your minds and you believe it. So now if I tell you that I am innocent — and Allah knows that I am innocent — you will not believe me; but if I admit something to you — and Allah knows that I am innocent — you will believe me. By Allah, I cannot find any example to give you except what the father of Yusuf said: *So patience is most fitting, and it is Allah Whose help can be sought against that which you describe*" (12:18).

Then she turned her face away and lay down on her bed, thinking herself far too insignificant for Allah to reveal Qur'an about her that would be recited forever; she only hoped the Prophet ﷺ might see a dream in which Allah proved her innocence. He had not moved from where he was sitting, and nobody had left the house, before revelation came down upon him, drops of sweat like pearls running down him even on a winter's day. When it passed he was smiling, and the first thing he said was: "Be glad, O 'A'ishah — Allah has declared your innocence." Her mother told her to get up and go to him. She said: by Allah, I will not go to him, and I will give praise to no one except Allah, for He is the One who has proven my innocence.

Since the accusers could produce no evidence, Ma'arif ul Qur'an adds, the Prophet ﷺ applied the hadd of qadhf, eighty lashes — citing Bazzar and Ibn Marduwaih from Abu Hurayrah that Mistah, Hamnah and Hassan were punished, and Tabarani from 'Umar that Ibn Ubayy received double. After that the Muslims repented; the hypocrites remained as they were.

## The word "ifk"

Ma'arif ul Qur'an explains that *ifk* literally means to turn over, to reverse, to change. It covers the worst kind of lie: the one that turns truth into falsehood and falsehood into truth. Ibn Kathir glosses it as lies, falsehood and fabrications.

*'Usbah* ("a group") means, per Ma'arif ul Qur'an, a band of ten to forty — Ibn Kathir says it means they were not one or two but a group, a gang among you, with Ibn Ubayy foremost among them. The sting is in *minkum*, "from among you": Ma'arif ul Qur'an notes that the actual fabricator, Ibn Ubayy, was a hypocrite and not truly a Muslim, but since the hypocrites claimed to be Muslims he too is included in "you".

Then the turn in ayah 11: **do not think it evil for you; rather it is good for you.** Ibn Kathir addresses this to the family of Abu Bakr — honourable mention in this world, raised status in the Hereafter. Ma'arif ul Qur'an widens it to the Prophet ﷺ, 'A'ishah, Safwan and all the Muslims hurt by the affair: what looked like ruin became the reason her purity is confirmed in ten ayat recited until the Day of Judgement. Ibn Kathir records that Ibn 'Abbas came to her as she was dying and said: rejoice — you are the wife of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he used to love you, he married no virgin other than you, and your innocence was revealed from heaven. And Ma'arif ul Qur'an cites Tafsir al-Qurtubi: Yusuf, falsely accused, was cleared by an infant granted speech; Maryam by her son 'Isa; 'A'ishah by ten ayat of the Qur'an itself.

The close of ayah 11 divides the guilty by degree: *each man among them will bear what he earned of the sin.* Ma'arif ul Qur'an spells out the gradation — the one who fabricated it deserves the most severe punishment, the one who endorsed it when it reached him a little less, the one who merely kept quiet after hearing it less still. As for *the one who took on the greater share of it*, Ibn Kathir reports two views: the one who initiated the rumours, or the one who collected them and spread them among the people; he identifies the man as Ibn Ubayy, as does Ma'arif ul Qur'an citing Baghawi.

## Ayah 12: the failure of the believers

Ayah 12 asks why the believers did not think well of their own people and say outright, "This is an obvious lie."

Ibn Kathir gives two readings. First: why did they not compare what was said to themselves — if such a thing would not befit them, it was even less appropriate for the Mother of the believers. Second, from Ibn Ishaq, that it was revealed about Abu Ayyub al-Ansari and his wife: when Umm Ayyub asked whether he had heard what people were saying, he answered, "Yes, and it is all lies. Would you do that, O Umm Ayyub?" She said, "No, by Allah, I would not do that." He said, "And by Allah, 'A'ishah is better than you."

Ma'arif ul Qur'an opens three points of language here. **"Of their own selves":** the ayah does not say "think well of her" but *think well on their own selves* (bi-anfusihim). The bond of Islam has brought Muslims together as one body, so a Muslim who defames another in fact disgraces himself. It links this to *do not cast aspersion on your own selves* (49:11) and *do not kill yourselves* (4:29) — each meaning your Muslim brethren, because harm to one Muslim's honour leads to the defamation of the whole Ummah.

**The change of address.** The ayah begins with "you" — *when you heard it* — then switches to the third person: *why did the believing men and women not think well*. Ma'arif ul Qur'an reads this as a subtle allusion: to the extent of this act they were not fit to be called believers, since faith demanded that a Muslim hold to the favourable view of another Muslim.

**The ruling.** From Mazhari, cited in Ma'arif ul Qur'an: it is obligatory to think well of all Muslim men and women unless the contrary is proved under Islamic law; and if someone accuses a Muslim without proof under Islamic law, rejecting that accusation and declaring it a lie is likewise obligatory — because it is nothing but backbiting and defaming an innocent Muslim.

## Ayah 13: where were the four witnesses?

Ayah 13 turns the community from gossip to procedure: *why did they not bring four witnesses?* And since they did not — *with Allah, they are the liars.*

Ma'arif ul Qur'an notes that since a charge of adultery cannot be proved without four eyewitnesses, they should have demanded four eyewitnesses or silence instead of becoming instruments in passing the rumour on. It then raises the obvious question: suppose a man genuinely saw something with his own eyes but cannot produce four witnesses — how is he "a liar with Allah", who knows exactly what happened? Two answers. First, "with Allah" stands for Allah's command and ruling: the rule is that you do not relate what you saw unless four witnesses are available, so one who relates it anyway is declared a liar by law and punished accordingly. Second, a Muslim should testify to another's sin only with the intent of controlling and eradicating evil, never to defame or hurt; one who publicises it without four witnesses can neither prove the crime under Islamic law nor see the accused punished — so his claim to be reforming society is itself the lie.

**Did the Prophet ﷺ fall short of this?** If good opinion is obligatory, why did he not deny the rumour at the outset, and why did he tell 'A'ishah to beg Allah's pardon if there had been a slip on her part (Bukhari)? Ma'arif ul Qur'an answers: he never affirmed the rumour, never acted on what it demanded, and disliked its spread; all he said in the gathering of the Companions was "I know nothing about my family but good" (Bukhari) — itself proof of acting on the very injunction these ayat give. Doubt and anxiety arise naturally in such a situation, and the definite certainty came when the ayat of exoneration were revealed. Those who were punished, by contrast, had acted on what the rumour demanded and had spread it.

## Ayat 14–15: "you thought it a small thing"

Ayah 14 tells those who had been talking that only Allah's grace and mercy in this world and the Hereafter stood between them and a great torment. Ibn Kathir: Allah accepted their repentance in this world and forgave them because of their faith in the Hereafter — this refers to believers such as Mistah, Hassan and Hamnah bint Jahsh, not to hypocrites like Ibn Ubayy and his like, who did not have sufficient faith and righteous deeds to balance out what they had done. Ma'arif ul Qur'an unpacks that grace as a chain: they were helped to Islam and its faith; given the company of the Prophet ﷺ, which is itself an impediment to punishment; then helped to repent sincerely and beg forgiveness; and finally their repentance was accepted and the sin pardoned.

Ayah 15 is a forensic description of how gossip works. *When you were receiving it with your tongues* — Ma'arif ul Qur'an says *talaqqa* means to make inquiries of one another and repeat before others: here, repeating hearsay without probe or proof. Mujahid and Sa'id bin Jubayr, quoted by Ibn Kathir, describe it exactly: some of you were relating it to others, one saying "I heard this from so-and-so, and so-and-so said such and such." Ibn Kathir notes that others recited the word as *taliqunahu*, "when you were inventing a lie with your tongues" — and it is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari that 'A'ishah recited it that way; the first recitation, he says, is preferred and the reading of the majority.

Then: *and you were saying with your mouths what you had no knowledge of. And you thought it a light thing, while with Allah it was very great.* Ibn Kathir: even if she had not been the Prophet's ﷺ wife it would still not be an insignificant matter — how then when she is the wife of the Seal of the Prophets and Leader of the Messengers ﷺ? Ma'arif ul Qur'an: in the sight of Allah it was a great sin to pass on to others, without probing or finding any proof, something that harms Muslims and makes their lives miserable. Ibn Kathir cites what is reported in the Two Sahihs: a man may say a word that angers Allah without realising how far it will go, and because of it be thrown into Hell a distance greater than that between heaven and earth.

## Ayat 16–17: the sentence you should have said

Ayah 16 supplies the exact words the believers should have used: *It is not right for us to speak of this. Glory be to You — this is a great lie.*

Ibn Kathir calls this a further stage of discipline beyond the command to think well: if Shaytan insinuates some unsuitable thought into a person's mind, he should not speak about it — for the Prophet ﷺ said, as reported in the Two Sahihs, that Allah will excuse this Ummah for whatever occurs to their minds so long as they do not speak about it or act upon it. And *Subhanaka* — "Glory be to You" — is the reflex of a heart that finds the accusation not merely false but obscene: glory be to Allah, says Ibn Kathir, that such a thing should be said about the wife of His Prophet and close Friend ﷺ. Ma'arif ul Qur'an adds that the believers should have said in categorical terms that they were not even allowed to mention a thing for which there is no proof.

Ma'arif ul Qur'an then answers one more doubt: if you cannot affirm a report without proof, how can you call it a lie without proof?
